items.headline: AMD returns as an acquirer rather than an earnings print, and yesterday's unclosed session now has a close
items.diff_narrative: AMD carries over as the same actor with a different kind of event attached. Yesterday it was an earnings story: second-quarter 2026 revenue of $11.5 billion, a data centre segment of $6.7 billion up 107% year over year, and a share move that yesterday's file could only take mid-session, given as down 4.33% in intraday trading on Wednesday, August 5 on a session that had not closed. Today that session has a settled number, and it is the larger one: AMD closed Wednesday at $482.05, down 7.04% for the session, then closed Thursday, August 6 at $489.28, up 1.50%. Today's sources do not attribute the Thursday move to anything in particular and neither should a reader. The event itself is a corporate action, not a shipment. AMD said on Thursday, August 6 that it has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Taalas, a Toronto company founded in 2023; no price was disclosed, the deal is subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals, and no closing date was given, so this is a signed agreement rather than a completed acquisition and nothing in the shipping line-up has moved. Taalas builds model-specific integrated circuits that embed a model's weights and dataflow into transistors instead of streaming them out of high-bandwidth memory, assembling a part of roughly 100 layers with only two metal layers customised per model, which it puts at a tape-out of about two months; its HC1 test part on TSMC's 6-nanometer process served Meta's Llama 3.1 8B at roughly 17,000 tokens per second. It raised $169 million in February 2026 from Quiet Capital, Fidelity and Pierre Lamond, taking total funding to about $219 million. One thread from yesterday stays open rather than closing. Yesterday's entry recorded that the print arrived without the quantified Helios rack-scale order figure that had been named as the second thing to read. Helios reappears today, but as an integration target rather than a number: AMD says it intends to fold the technology into its accelerator roadmap and build system-level products pairing it with Instinct GPUs, Helios rackscale systems, EPYC CPUs and ROCm. Yesterday's AMD item was set up to test whether enterprise AI spend converts into recognised revenue; today's asks a different question, what a serving part looks like once the model is fixed and cost per token is the only variable left.

items.headline: Liquid AI's LFM2.5-2.6B puts a tool-calling agent loop under 2.5 GB of memory
items.diff_narrative: Nothing in yesterday's file touched on-device models, so this opens a thread rather than advancing one. Liquid AI published LFM2.5-2.6B on Tuesday, August 4, which means today is when it enters this corpus rather than when it shipped. The model is 2.6 billion parameters, pre-trained on roughly 34 trillion tokens with the context window extended to 128K mid-training, and aimed at agent work — planning, tool calls, multi-step tasks — that completes on the device instead of round-tripping to a hosted API. The claim that carries is the footprint: under 2.5 GB of memory, with measurements of 220 tokens per second on an Apple M5 Max, 113 tokens per second on an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, and close to 15,000 output tokens per second on a single NVIDIA H100 under high concurrency. On the ToolSandbox tool-use benchmark it reports 77.83 against 65.00 for Gemma 4 E4B-it and 52.40 for Gemma 4 E2B-it, plus a Claw-Eval English average of 62.85 and a lead over its comparison set on IFBench, Multi-IF and IFStruct. Release-day runtime support covers llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang and ONNX, with transformers 5.0.0 or later. The hedge belongs in the same breath and today's file states it: every one of those figures is the vendor's own, published alongside the model rather than independently reproduced, so the memory ceiling is the durable part and the benchmark ordering is not. Read against yesterday, this is the opposite direction of travel on the same exposure. Yesterday's platform entry was Cloudflare putting per-service Gatekeeper Workers between an agent and a system of record, which is authorisation added at a boundary; an agent loop small enough to run locally removes one of the boundary crossings instead of policing it. Neither displaces the other, but they are answers to the same question from opposite ends.

items.headline: Meta ships Muse Code in beta; separately, Herdr relicenses its command-line agent runtime from AGPL to Apache-2.0
items.diff_narrative: Coding agents appeared in yesterday's file only as an explanation for someone else's exit — the Flowise sunset notice reasoned that as models got better at reasoning, developers moved to coding agents and the rigid low-code approach hit its ceiling. Today two entries put products against that explanation. Meta's research group published Muse Code and Muse Spark 1.2 on Wednesday, August 5, the same date as yesterday's file, which did not carry them. Muse Code is a terminal coding agent and it is explicitly in beta, installed on macOS and Linux by piping an install script from dev.meta.ai; beta is the status to hold onto, because nothing here is a general-availability release. Two design choices are worth lifting out for anyone building a comparable harness: the subagents are asynchronous and persist for the whole session rather than being spawned per task, and they decide themselves when to report back, which is what removes round-trip latency from multi-step problems; and every model call, tool run, approval and edit is appended to a local event log, which Meta describes as making the agent replay-exact and restart-safe so that a crash resumes precisely where it stopped. Muse Spark 1.2 is the model underneath, available now inside Muse Code and through the Meta Model API; the announcement names Terminal-Bench 2.1, DeepSWE 1.1 and an internal coding benchmark as its comparisons but does not state the scores, so there is no number here to set against anything. The second entry is a separate project at the other end of the size range, and nothing in either announcement ties the two together. Herdr said on Thursday, August 6 that it has joined Y Combinator's F26 batch and, in the same post, relicensed its terminal runtime for command-line coding agents from AGPL to Apache-2.0, with no funding figure given. It is a shell agents run inside rather than an agent itself: it organises command-line coding agents into panes, tabs and projects and keeps them running persistently on whichever machine it is installed on, including a remote host it installs itself onto over ssh, with those machines disconnected from each other today. The licence move is the load-bearing part for anyone already embedding it, because AGPL's network-use clause is what would have obliged a hosted service built on Herdr to publish its own source; Apache-2.0 removes that obligation, which widens who can adopt the runtime and gives away the only thing that had reserved the hosted layer, leaving the paid tier it intends to sell defended by nothing but execution and being first. One thing to notice against yesterday's length on agent boundaries: Meta presents the event log as crash recovery, not as an audit control, and a replay-exact record of every approval is exactly what an incident investigation like the institute's would have wanted.

items.headline: An approval game with more than 40,000 runs puts a distribution around the human in the approval loop
items.diff_narrative: This has no prior-day antecedent but it is the empirical counterpart to the item yesterday's file led with. Yesterday's incident turned on a permission granted without a rule about what it was for; today measures what happens when the rule exists and a person has to apply it one command at a time. Alex Wauters published the analysis on the Scale X blog on Wednesday, August 5 — another Wednesday artifact arriving a day late — covering an interactive browser game in which the player is the human approver for a coding agent under time pressure. Across more than 40,000 runs and roughly 409,000 approve-or-deny decisions, mean accuracy was 66.3%, and the miss rate tracked how much a hostile command looked like one: 11.7% for obviously destructive commands, 23.8% for persistent mutation attacks, 33.4% for exfiltration and code execution, 35.0% for scope violations. 35.2% of players caught every threat, but only 20.8% managed that while blocking no more than one in five safe commands; 7% approved everything put in front of them and 32.9% of sessions ended on a negative score. The single most-missed command was npm run analyze, approved 64.7% of the time even though the malicious payload was visible in the history log. The author's caveat is in the source and it cuts both ways: threats appeared in 34% of commands, far above any real workload, and a timed game is not a working day, but a real operator meets the hostile command more rarely and is therefore less primed for it. The join to yesterday is precise rather than rhetorical. Yesterday's file recorded a human maintainer who did spot the malicious change put in front of him and refused to approve it, which is the point at which the institute's incident stopped. Today's file puts a distribution around that maintainer: the check holds at 66.3% mean accuracy across 409,000 decisions, and it fails most often exactly where the hostile command looks least like one. The author's conclusion — put the check in the tool layer, where the payload is inspected, rather than in the approval prompt, where only the command line is — arrives at the same place as yesterday's Gatekeeper item from the other side.

items.headline: Cisco publishes twelve advisories on a pre-announced date, with three Catalyst SD-WAN identifiers at 9.9
items.diff_narrative: Security carries over from yesterday but comes in through a different door. Yesterday's entry was a catalogue of things already being exploited with a government deadline attached: CISA added three vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on Tuesday, August 4 with a federal remediation date of Friday, August 7, which is now tomorrow. Today's entry is a scheduled vendor disclosure. Cisco's product security incident response team published twelve advisories on Wednesday, August 5 — two critical, four high and six medium — covering Catalyst SD-WAN Software, IOS XE, IOS, the Integrated Management Controller, RoomOS and the Terminal Services Agent. The one to work first is the Catalyst SD-WAN security hardening release, which carries five identifiers: CVE-2026-20303, CVE-2026-20304 and CVE-2026-20310 at CVSS 9.9, CVE-2026-20312 at 8.8 and CVE-2026-20313 at 7.7. Cisco states these affect Catalyst SD-WAN Software regardless of device configuration, that there are no workarounds, and that it is not aware of any public announcements or malicious use of them; fixed releases are 20.9.10, 20.12.8.1, 20.15.6, 20.18.4 and 26.1.2 depending on the branch, against vulnerable trains running from before 20.9.1 through 20.18 plus release 26.1. The second critical advisory is the IOS XE security hardening release at CVSS 9.8. What separates the two days is what sets the clock, not the counts, which measure different things and should not be set against each other: today's twelve came out of one vendor's internal testing, with an advance notification posted on Wednesday, July 29 naming the publication date a week ahead, so the maintenance window was schedulable; yesterday's three were catalogue additions across three vendors driven by exploitation observed in the wild, with the deadline coming from the government rather than from the vendor. A coincidence worth not over-reading sits between them: yesterday's Langflow flaw was published at CVSS 9.8 and today's IOS XE hardening release is also at 9.8, but one is on the exploited list and the other is explicitly not. And set against yesterday's other security entry, the six fabricated SQLite advisories that cleared the national feed unchallenged, today's batch is the far end of the same distribution — named fixed releases, a dated advance notice and a stated exploitation status, which is what a feed entry does not give you.

items.headline: Unsloth rejoins the file after a day out with five package releases in three days and DSpark on by default
items.diff_narrative: This is a continuation with a gap in it, and the gap is worth stating rather than papering over: the Unsloth thread ran on Monday, August 3 and Tuesday, August 4 and did not appear in yesterday's file at all, so today rejoins the storyline rather than advancing it from yesterday. Tuesday's entry was about one very large Studio merge with no package behind it, and it recorded two specific absences — the Python library still sat at 2026.8.2 on PyPI and the documentation changelog had not moved past July 29. Both have now moved. PyPI carries 2026.8.3 dated Tuesday, August 4, 2026.8.4 dated Wednesday, August 5, and 2026.8.5, 2026.8.6 and 2026.8.7 all dated Thursday, August 6 — five releases across three days, three of them on today alone — with a changelog entry against each. The content is thinner than the count, and that is the real diff. 2026.8.3 and 2026.8.6 are logged as fixes only, 2026.8.4 as training fixes and 2026.8.5 as Windows installation fixes; the only entry with shape to it is 2026.8.7, which lists DSpark support for DeepSeek-V4 Flash 0731 and a full rework of the training page. DSpark itself arrived earlier in the week, in the Studio release tagged v0.1.524-beta on Tuesday, August 4, where the notes say it is now on by default and describe it as doubling inference speed — with no tokens-per-second figure published on either side of that comparison, so the claimed multiple cannot be checked from the project's own material and should be carried as a vendor claim, not a measurement. That same release shipped DeepSeek-V4 Flash 0731 quantisations from 83 GB at UD-IQ1_S to 162 GB at UD-Q8_K_XL, support for Moonshot's Kimi K3 — a 2.8-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 104 billion active parameters, native vision and a one-million-token context window — and an automatic fallback from XET to plain HTTP when a download stalls, continuing the download-reliability work already logged against 2026.8.2. Across the week the shape changes from one large capability merge to a run of maintenance releases: the training-page rework is the only change a user would notice, and what grew is the release count, not the surface.

items.headline: Bay Area / SV AI meet-up events: Las Vegas turns over, the price step lands tomorrow, and a Palo Alto meetup comes back verified
items.diff_narrative: Las Vegas turns over. Yesterday Black Hat's Briefings were opening and Ai4 and FMS were listed as closing tomorrow; today all three close, Black Hat on the second and last day of its two-day main conference at the Mandalay Bay Convention Center, and BSides Las Vegas with its first dedicated AI-security track finished on Wednesday as yesterday said it would. DEF CON 34 moves from opening tomorrow to open, running at the LVCC West Hall through Sunday, August 9, and it is now the only thing left standing in that city. Its details change register rather than fact: today keeps the $520 in cash at the door and names the queue, LineCon, while dropping the hotel-block inventory and the July 31 pre-registration cutoff yesterday carried; the AI Village becomes LVCC L1 W603 rather than Room W603; HalCTF's hosted model range is restated as 2.1B to 120B rather than 2B to 120B and its score decay is now specified as linear, with the rest identical — teams of up to five, an agent container capped at 2.5 GB, bonus points for winning with smaller models and a DGX Spark for first place. The nearest money deadline advances by exactly one day and does not move in price: SecurityWeek's AI Risk Summit full pass is still $1,895 through Friday, August 7 and $2,195 after, with today's account putting the step explicitly at Saturday, August 8, so what yesterday called the nearest deadline on the list now falls tomorrow. The AI Agent Security Summit is unchanged and still lists exactly two open editions, submissions to Monday, August 17 for London on Thursday, October 8 and Friday, August 21 for New York on Wednesday, October 21 — the same position yesterday reached after an uncorroborated Tokyo date came out. Elsewhere detail moves in both directions. Gained: the AI Infra Summit picks up 400 speakers, 250 partners and eight stages alongside the 8,000 attendance figure it already had; the AI Conference's sold-out September 29 workshop-and-hack day gains a capacity, 350 seats; Ray Summit's co-located vLLM Conference was already stated to be included on every pass and today adds the span, all three days; and the Humanoids decision calendar gains weekday names on all five of its dates. Carried more thinly today rather than changed in the world: Hot Chips keeps the Sunday, August 16 housing deadline and the Wednesday, August 19 cancellation date but loses the 11:59 PM PDT hour and the $25 processing fee; OWASP loses its dated training window and its 800-plus attendance figure; and GTC Berlin loses STATION-Berlin, the Jensen Huang keynote and the 10,000-plus expected attendance. Standing still, which on a list this long is its own kind of information: the two summits that collide on Thursday, October 15 carry over intact, the separately-run AI Security Summit's San Francisco edition with its leadership and practitioner tracks, and the free, closed-door, practitioner-led session that despite its San Francisco name sits at the Crowne Plaza Palo Alto from 8:30 AM to 3:30 PM with its speakers already set rather than an open call. Same pair, same collision, no movement in either direction. The AI Tinkerers picture is the sharpest change, and for once it moves upward. Yesterday four meetups sitting beyond the calendar's last dated entry were downgraded to unverified on one shared piece of evidence: Palo Alto on Tuesday, August 18, Orange County on Wednesday, August 19, Boston on Thursday, September 3 and Columbus on Monday, September 7. Today Palo Alto is back, listed on the global calendar as a 6:30 to 9 PM PDT session rather than resting on a chapter page that was refusing requests, and two more entries joined the same Tuesday — Manchester, New Hampshire at 5:30 to 7:45 PM EDT and a Seattle Women in AI builders track at 5 to 8 PM PDT with lightning demos and code audits. The calendar's horizon moves with them, from the London hackathon on Sunday, August 16 to Tuesday, August 18. The other three of yesterday's four do not appear in today's account, so one of the four was resolved and three were not. The nearest session moves by the simplest mechanism on the list, the clock: the Los Angeles builder meetup and live demos that yesterday's file carried for Thursday, August 6 is tonight's session, 6 to 8 PM PDT, and today's account adds that it has already rolled off the calendar's forward list because it starts today. One entry goes the other way, in the pattern yesterday's Singapore session set: the Medellin voice-AI session the calendar had held for Friday, August 7 no longer appears and is now treated as unscheduled. Near-term sessions otherwise gain detail rather than dates — tomorrow's New York hack is Vision Hack v.2 with Google Cloud and Roboflow, Saturday's Mombasa chapter launch is on edge AI, local small models and autonomous swarms, and the Riyadh session on Saturday, August 15 is a Claude Code workshop. Nothing is dated in San Francisco, San Jose or Pleasanton, which is where yesterday left it.
